records.source: דְּבַר־יְהוָ֣ה׀אֲשֶׁ֣ר הָיָ֗ה אֶל־מִיכָה֙ הַמֹּ֣רַשְׁתִּ֔י בִּימֵ֥י יוֹתָ֛ם אָחָ֥ז יְחִזְקִיָּ֖ה מַלְכֵ֣י יְהוּדָ֑ה אֲשֶׁר־חָזָ֥ה עַל־שֹׁמְר֖וֹן וִירֽוּשָׁלִָֽם׃
records.gloss: [The] word of Yahweh which came to Micah the Morashtite in [the] days of Jotham, Ahaz, Hezekiah, kings of Judah, which he saw concerning Samaria and Jerusalem.
pieces: {{divine_name:The LORD|Yahweh}}'s word came to Micah of Moresheth during the reigns of Jotham, Ahaz, and Hezekiah over Judah. It is what he saw concerning Samaria and Jerusalem.

L.1: The word of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} which came to Micah the Morashtite in the days of Jotham, Ahaz, Hezekiah, kings of Judah, which he saw concerning Samaria and Jerusalem.

R.1: This is the message {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} gave to Micah from the town of Moresheth. It came while Jotham, Ahaz, and Hezekiah were kings of Judah. Micah saw these things about Samaria and Jerusalem.

decisions.choice: Micah the Morashtite: Micah from Moresheth, a town in the low hills southwest of Jerusalem
decisions.reason: Micah is named after his home town, Moresheth-gath (1:14), in the low hill country between Judah's mountains and the Philistine plain, near Gath. Jeremiah 26:18 calls him by the same title and quotes 3:12. His name means "Who is like the LORD?", and the book ends by asking "Who is a God like you?" (7:18).

decisions.choice: in the days of Jotham, Ahaz, Hezekiah: the second half of the eighth century BC
decisions.reason: These three kings of Judah reigned one after another from about 750 to 686 BC (2 Kings 15:32-20:21). Micah was a younger contemporary of Isaiah and Hosea (Isaiah 1:1; Hosea 1:1). Samaria, the capital of the northern kingdom, fell to Assyria in 722 BC, and Assyria invaded Judah in 701 BC, in Hezekiah's reign. Jeremiah 26:18-19 says that Micah spoke in Hezekiah's days and that Hezekiah heeded him.

decisions.choice: which he saw: the word given to the prophet as something seen
decisions.reason: The verb is used for a prophet's vision, and books of prophecy use it of the whole message, words included (Isaiah 1:1; Amos 1:1). Samaria and Jerusalem were the capitals of the two kingdoms, Israel in the north and Judah in the south, and they stand for the two peoples. The book speaks to both.

decisions.choice: The word of the LORD that came to (L); the LORD's word came to (B); This is the message the LORD gave to (R); during the reigns of (B); while ... were kings (R); of Moresheth (B); from the town of Moresheth (R)
decisions.reason: The heading follows the formula set for the first verse of each of the Twelve, as in Hosea 1:1 and Joel 1:1. Balanced and Readable name Micah's home town as Jeremiah 26:18 does at those levels, rather than use the word formed from it.

records.heading: {{divine_name:The LORD|Yahweh}} comes against Samaria and Jerusalem

records.source: שִׁמְעוּ֙ עַמִּ֣ים כֻּלָּ֔ם הַקְשִׁ֖יבִי אֶ֣רֶץ וּמְלֹאָ֑הּ וִיהִי֩ אֲדֹנָ֨י יְהוִ֤ה בָּכֶם֙ לְעֵ֔ד אֲדֹנָ֖י מֵהֵיכַ֥ל קָדְשֽׁוֹ׃
records.gloss: Hear, peoples, all of them; pay attention, earth and what fills it, and let be [the] Lord Yahweh against you for a witness, [the] Lord from [the] temple of his holiness.
pieces: Listen, all you peoples; \q pay attention, earth and everything in it! \q Let the Lord {{divine_name:GOD|Yahweh}} be a witness against you, \q the Lord from {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} holy temple.

L.2: Hear, peoples, all of them; \q pay attention, earth and all that fills it, \q and let the Lord {{divine_name:GOD|Yahweh}} be a witness against you, \q the Lord from {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} holy temple.

R.2: Listen, all you nations! \q Pay attention, earth and everyone on it! \q The Lord {{divine_name:GOD|Yahweh}} will speak as a witness against you. \q The Lord speaks from {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} holy temple.

decisions.choice: Hear, peoples, all of them: the same words as 1 Kings 22:28
decisions.reason: The prophet Micaiah son of Imlah ends his warning to King Ahab with these words (1 Kings 22:28; 2 Chronicles 18:27). Micah, whose name is a short form of Micaiah, opens his book with them. The call goes out to all the peoples and to the whole earth, as Isaiah 1:2 calls heaven and earth to listen.

decisions.choice: a witness against you: the Lord testifies against those he summons
decisions.reason: The words picture a court. The nations and the earth are called to hear, and the Lord himself takes the stand as witness. The preposition may mean "against you" or "among you". "Against" fits the court and the judgment that follows; the case the LORD brings is against Samaria and Jerusalem (verse 5), and the nations hear it as a warning that he judges the whole earth. The text does not say whether "you" means the peoples or Israel.

decisions.choice: his holy temple: the LORD's dwelling in heaven
decisions.reason: In the next verse the LORD comes out from "his place" and comes down to the earth, so the temple here is his dwelling above, as in Psalm 11:4 ("The LORD is in his holy temple; the LORD's throne is in heaven") and Habakkuk 2:20. The earthly temple in Jerusalem was its copy, and later in the book it too is judged (3:12).

decisions.choice: Hear, peoples, all of them (L); Listen, all you peoples (B); all you nations (R); all that fills it (L); everything in it (B); everyone on it (R)
decisions.reason: Literal and Balanced keep the wording of 1 Kings 22:28 at those levels. Readable says "nations", the plain word for peoples, and turns the wish "let the Lord be a witness" into a statement of what he is about to do.

records.source: כִּֽי־הִנֵּ֥ה יְהוָ֖ה יֹצֵ֣א מִמְּקוֹמ֑וֹ וְיָרַ֥ד וְדָרַ֖ךְ עַל־בָּ֥מֳתֵי אָֽרֶץ׃
records.gloss: For look, Yahweh [is] going out from his place, and he will come down and tread on [the] high places of [the] earth.
pieces: See, {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} is coming out from {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} dwelling; \q {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} will come down and tread on the heights of the earth.

L.3: For look, {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} is coming out from {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} place, \q and {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} will come down and tread on the earth's heights.

R.3: Look! {{divine_name:The LORD|Yahweh}} is leaving {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} home in heaven. \q He will come down and walk on the high places of the earth.

decisions.choice: tread on the heights of the earth: the words of Amos 4:13, where the LORD is the Creator who walks over the mountains
decisions.reason: Amos uses the same phrase in a hymn to the LORD as Creator (Amos 4:13), and Deuteronomy 32:13 and 33:29 speak of riding or treading on the heights as a mark of mastery. To tread on the heights is to rule over the whole earth. When the LORD comes down, the earth cannot bear his coming (verse 4).

decisions.choice: high places: the heights of the land, with a hint of the hilltop shrines
decisions.reason: The word means heights or ridges. It is also the usual word for the hilltop shrines where Israel and Judah worshiped, often with idols, and verse 5 uses it in that sense: "the high places of Judah". The LORD comes down onto the very heights where he is falsely worshiped.

decisions.choice: coming out from his place: the LORD comes to judge
decisions.reason: "His place" is his dwelling in heaven (verse 2). Scripture often pictures God coming down to see and to act (Genesis 11:5; Exodus 19:18-20; Isaiah 26:21, where he comes "out of his place" to punish the earth). Here his coming is a judgment: the mountains melt under him.

decisions.choice: the earth's heights (L), the heights of the earth (B), walk on the high places of the earth (R), as Amos 4:13; his home in heaven (R)
decisions.reason: Each level reuses its wording of Amos 4:13. Readable says where "his place" is (m3).

records.source: וְנָמַ֤סּוּ הֶֽהָרִים֙ תַּחְתָּ֔יו וְהָעֲמָקִ֖ים יִתְבַּקָּ֑עוּ כַּדּוֹנַג֙ מִפְּנֵ֣י הָאֵ֔שׁ כְּמַ֖יִם מֻגָּרִ֥ים בְּמוֹרָֽד׃
records.gloss: And will melt the mountains under him, and the valleys will split open, like wax before the fire, like water poured down on a slope.
pieces: The mountains will melt beneath {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}, \q and the valleys will burst apart, \q like wax before the fire, \q like water rushing down a steep slope.

L.4: And the mountains will melt under {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}, \q and the valleys will split open, \q like wax before the fire, \q like water poured down a slope.

R.4: The mountains will melt under {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} feet. \q The valleys will split open. \q The mountains will melt like wax near a fire. \q The valleys will pour away like water rushing down a hill.

decisions.choice: mountains melting like wax: a picture used when God comes
decisions.reason: Psalm 97:5 says that the mountains melt like wax before the LORD, and Judges 5:4-5 and Psalm 68:9 tell how the earth shook when God came out from Sinai. Nahum 1:5 uses the same picture. Nothing in creation stands firm when its maker comes to judge.

decisions.choice: like wax ... like water: the first likeness goes with the mountains, the second with the valleys
decisions.reason: Hebrew poetry often matches two pictures with two things in order. The mountains melt like wax in a fire, and the valleys split open as water cuts a channel when it pours down a slope.

decisions.choice: under his feet; The mountains will melt ... The valleys will pour away (R)
decisions.reason: Readable says which likeness goes with which part of the land (m2), so that the two pictures are not left floating. "Under his feet" says what "under him" means when he treads on the heights (verse 3).

records.source: בְּפֶ֤שַׁע יַֽעֲקֹב֙ כָּל־זֹ֔את וּבְחַטֹּ֖אות בֵּ֣ית יִשְׂרָאֵ֑ל מִֽי־פֶ֣שַׁע יַעֲקֹ֗ב הֲלוֹא֙ שֹֽׁמְר֔וֹן וּמִי֙ בָּמ֣וֹת יְהוּדָ֔ה הֲל֖וֹא יְרוּשָׁלִָֽם׃
records.gloss: For [the] transgression of Jacob [is] all this, and for [the] sins of [the] house of Israel. Who [is the] transgression of Jacob? [Is it] not Samaria? And who [are the] high places of Judah? [Is it] not Jerusalem?
pieces: All this is because of Jacob's rebellion \q and because of the sins of the house of Israel. \q What is Jacob's rebellion? Is it not Samaria? \q And what are Judah's high places? \q Are they not Jerusalem?

L.5: All this [is] for the transgression of Jacob \q and for the sins of the house of Israel. \q Who [is] the transgression of Jacob? [Is it] not Samaria? \q And who [are] the high places of Judah? \q [Are they] not Jerusalem?

R.5: All this will happen because the people of Jacob have sinned, \q because the people of Israel have done wrong. \q Who is to blame for Jacob's sin? Is it not Samaria? \q Who is to blame for Judah's hilltop shrines? \q Is it not Jerusalem?

decisions.choice: Who is the transgression of Jacob? The capital cities are named as the source of the nation's sin
decisions.reason: The question asks "who", not "what": the sin is identified with a place and its people. Samaria and Jerusalem, the capitals where the kings, the officials and the chief shrines were, are where the wrong began and from where it spread. Here "Jacob" pairs with Samaria and means the northern kingdom, and Judah pairs with Jerusalem. In the first half of the verse "Jacob" and "the house of Israel" may mean the whole people.

decisions.choice: transgression: rebellion, a breaking of faith with God
decisions.reason: The word means a revolt, the act of a subject who breaks away from his overlord (2 Kings 8:20). Used of Israel, it is rebellion against the LORD, who made a covenant with them. Verse 13 and 3:8 use it again.

decisions.choice: the high places of Judah: as the Hebrew text has it
alternatives: the sin of the house of Judah
decisions.reason: The Hebrew text has "the high places of Judah", the hilltop shrines (see verse 3). The ancient Greek translation and some other ancient versions read "the sin of the house of Judah", which matches the first half of the verse more closely. The Hebrew is the harder reading, and it fits the charge in verse 7 that the shrines were places of idolatry, so it is kept.

decisions.choice: transgression (L); rebellion (B); sin (R); high places (L, B); hilltop shrines (R); Who is to blame for (R)
decisions.reason: The word for transgression follows the wording set for the prophets. Readable says what the high places were and puts the question "who is ...?" as "who is to blame for ...?", which is its point (m1). Balanced asks "what", as English would, since a city is named in the answer.

records.source: וְשַׂמְתִּ֥י שֹׁמְר֛וֹן לְעִ֥י הַשָּׂדֶ֖ה לְמַטָּ֣עֵי כָ֑רֶם וְהִגַּרְתִּ֤י לַגַּי֙ אֲבָנֶ֔יהָ וִיסֹדֶ֖יהָ אֲגַלֶּֽה׃
records.gloss: And I will make Samaria into a heap of ruins of the field, into planting places of a vineyard; and I will pour down to the valley her stones, and her foundations I will uncover.
pieces: So I will make Samaria a heap of rubble in the open country, a place for planting vineyards. \q I will hurl her stones down into the valley \q and lay her foundations bare.

L.6: And I will make Samaria a heap of ruins in the field, a place for planting vineyards; \q and I will pour down her stones into the valley \q and uncover her foundations.

R.6: So I will turn Samaria into a pile of rubble in an open field, a place to plant grapevines. \q I will roll the stones of her buildings down into the valley \q and leave her foundations showing.

decisions.choice: I will make: the LORD now speaks
decisions.reason: Verses 2-5 speak about the LORD; here he speaks himself, as often in the prophets, without a formula to mark the change. The poem's "I" is the LORD until verse 8, where the prophet speaks of his own grief.

decisions.choice: Samaria will become a field for vineyards: the city on its hill will be leveled
decisions.reason: Samaria stood on a hill with steep sides (1 Kings 16:24). Its stones will be tumbled down the slopes into the valley below, and the hilltop will be fit only for planting vines, like any open field. Samaria fell to Assyria in 722 BC (2 Kings 17:5-6). "Her" is the city, which Hebrew speaks of as a woman.

decisions.choice: a heap of ruins (L); a heap of rubble (B); a pile of rubble (R); pour down (L); hurl (B); roll the stones of her buildings (R)
decisions.reason: The verb means to pour out, here of stones tipped over the edge of the hill. Balanced says "hurl" and Readable "roll", and Readable says that the stones are the city's buildings.

records.source: וְכָל־פְּסִילֶ֣יהָ יֻכַּ֗תּוּ וְכָל־אֶתְנַנֶּ֨יהָ֙ יִשָּׂרְפ֣וּ בָאֵ֔שׁ וְכָל־עֲצַבֶּ֖יהָ אָשִׂ֣ים שְׁמָמָ֑ה כִּ֠י מֵאֶתְנַ֤ן זוֹנָה֙ קִבָּ֔צָה וְעַד־אֶתְנַ֥ן זוֹנָ֖ה יָשֽׁוּבוּ׃
records.gloss: And all her carved images will be beaten to pieces, and all her hires will be burned with fire, and all her idols I will make a desolation; for from [the] hire of a prostitute she gathered [them], and to [the] hire of a prostitute they will return.
pieces: All her carved idols will be smashed to pieces, all her temple gifts burned in the fire, \q and I will lay waste all her images. \q For she collected them from a prostitute's pay, \q and they will go back to be a prostitute's pay.

L.7: And all her carved images will be beaten to pieces, and all her wages will be burned with fire, \q and all her idols I will make a desolation; \q for from the wages of a prostitute she gathered [them], \q and to the wages of a prostitute they will return.

R.7: All her idols will be smashed, and all the gifts given at her shrines will be burned. \q I will destroy all her false gods. \q She got them the way a prostitute gets her pay, \q and they will be used again to pay prostitutes.

decisions.choice: wages of a prostitute: the gifts offered at the shrines, pictured as a prostitute's fee
decisions.reason: The word is the payment given to a prostitute (Deuteronomy 23:19). Hosea uses it of the grain and wine Israel thought its idols had given it (Hosea 2:14; 9:1). Here "her wages" stand beside her images and idols, so they are the gifts and valuables given at the shrines, perhaps the silver and gold the idols were overlaid with. Worshiping other gods is pictured as prostitution, unfaithfulness to the LORD.

decisions.choice: from a prostitute's wages ... to a prostitute's wages: what was gathered by unfaithfulness will be spent the same way
decisions.reason: The line turns on itself. Samaria built up her shrines with gifts gained in false worship; the enemy will carry them off, and they will again become offerings in a foreign temple, or pay for its prostitutes. Either way, what came from false worship goes back to it, and Samaria keeps nothing. The text does not say exactly how they will return.

decisions.choice: carved images ... idols: two words for the images of false gods
decisions.reason: The first word means an image carved from wood or stone, the second an idol of any kind, a word related to the word for pain or toil. Together with the shrine gifts they name everything Samaria's false worship had gathered.

decisions.choice: wages (L); temple gifts, a prostitute's pay (B); the gifts given at her shrines, the way a prostitute gets her pay (R)
decisions.reason: Literal keeps one word, "wages", for all three uses so that the repetition shows. Balanced and Readable say what "her wages" were (m1), and keep the picture of a prostitute's pay in the second half.

records.source: עַל־זֹאת֙ אֶסְפְּדָ֣ה וְאֵילִ֔ילָה אֵילְכָ֥ה שׁוֹלָ֖ל וְעָר֑וֹם אֶעֱשֶׂ֤ה מִסְפֵּד֙ כַּתַּנִּ֔ים וְאֵ֖בֶל כִּבְנ֥וֹת יַעֲנָֽה׃
records.gloss: On this I will lament and I will wail; I will go barefoot and naked; I will make a lament like jackals and a mourning like [the] daughters of an ostrich.
pieces: For this I will mourn and wail; \q I will go about barefoot and stripped. \q I will howl like the jackals \q and mourn like the ostriches.

L.8: Because of this I will lament and wail; \q I will go barefoot and naked; \q I will make a lament like the jackals \q and mourning like the ostriches.

R.8: Because of this I will mourn and cry aloud. \q I will walk around barefoot and stripped of my clothes. \q I will howl like a jackal \q and cry like an ostrich.

decisions.choice: I will lament: the prophet himself now speaks
decisions.reason: The grief is the prophet's. He mourns over the judgment he has announced, which has now reached his own people (verse 9). Jeremiah grieves in the same way (Jeremiah 4:19; 8:21).

decisions.choice: barefoot and naked: stripped like a mourner or a captive
decisions.reason: Mourners went barefoot (2 Samuel 15:30), and prisoners of war were led away barefoot and stripped (Isaiah 20:2-4, where Isaiah walks "naked and barefoot" as a sign of the captivity to come). "Naked" means without the outer garment, wearing only what was underneath. The first word is spelled one way in the written text and read another way, as noted in the margin; the reading means barefoot or stripped (Job 12:17, 19).

decisions.choice: jackals ... ostriches: creatures of the wilderness, known for their cries
decisions.reason: Jackals howl at night, and the ostrich makes a loud, mournful call. Both live in deserted places and belong to pictures of ruin (Isaiah 13:21-22; Job 30:29). The Hebrew says "daughters of the ostrich", a common way of naming the bird; some take it to be an owl.

decisions.choice: naked (L); stripped (B); stripped of my clothes (R); like the ostriches
decisions.reason: Literal keeps "naked"; Balanced and Readable say "stripped", which is what the word means here (m2). The "daughters of the ostrich" are simply ostriches, as the expression means.

records.source: כִּ֥י אֲנוּשָׁ֖ה מַכּוֹתֶ֑יהָ כִּי־בָ֨אָה֙ עַד־יְהוּדָ֔ה נָגַ֛ע עַד־שַׁ֥עַר עַמִּ֖י עַד־יְרוּשָׁלִָֽם׃
records.gloss: For incurable [are] her wounds; for it has come to Judah; it has reached to [the] gate of my people, to Jerusalem.
pieces: For her wound cannot be healed; \q it has spread to Judah. \q It has reached the gate of my people, Jerusalem itself.

L.9: For her wounds [are] incurable, \q for it has come to Judah; \q it has reached to the gate of my people, to Jerusalem.

R.9: Samaria's wound cannot be healed. \q The disaster has spread to Judah. \q It has reached Jerusalem, the gate where my people live.

decisions.choice: her wounds are incurable ... it has come: Samaria's death blow spreads south to Judah
decisions.reason: "Her" is Samaria (verse 6). The noun is plural but the word "incurable" is singular, as if the blows were one wound; the verb "it has come" also has the wound, or the disaster, as its subject. The judgment that falls on Samaria will not stop at the border.

decisions.choice: the gate of my people: Jerusalem, the city where Judah gathers
decisions.reason: A city's gate was where its people met, traded and held court; to reach the gate is to reach the city itself. The prophet calls Judah "my people", his own. Assyria's army did reach Jerusalem in 701 BC but did not take it (2 Kings 18:13-19:36).

decisions.choice: her wound (B); Samaria's wound, The disaster (R)
decisions.reason: Balanced says "wound" in the singular, as the grammar treats it (m1). Readable names Samaria and says what has spread.

records.source: בְּגַת֙ אַל־תַּגִּ֔ידוּ בָּכ֖וֹ אַל־תִּבְכּ֑וּ בְּבֵ֣ית לְעַפְרָ֔ה עָפָ֖ר הִתְפַּלָּֽשִׁי׃
records.gloss: In Gath do not tell; weeping, do not weep; in Beth-leaphrah in dust roll yourself.
pieces: Do not tell it in Gath; \q do not weep at all. \q In Beth-leaphrah, roll in the dust.

L.10: Do not tell [it] in Gath; \q do not weep at all. \q In Beth-leaphrah roll yourself in [the] dust.

R.10: Do not tell the news in Gath. \q Do not let your enemies see you cry. \q In Beth-leaphrah, the House of Dust, roll in the dust to show your sorrow.

decisions.choice: Do not tell it in Gath: the words of David's lament for Saul and Jonathan
decisions.reason: David began his lament with "Do not tell it in Gath" (2 Samuel 1:20), so that the Philistines would not gloat over Israel's defeat. Micah takes up the line as he begins to mourn over the towns of his own district. In Hebrew the name Gath sounds like the verb "tell", the first of the wordplays on place names that run through verses 10-15.

decisions.choice: do not weep at all: as the Hebrew text reads
decisions.reason: The Hebrew doubles the verb for emphasis, "weeping, do not weep". Since every other line in these verses names a town, some read the first word as a place name, "in Acco" or "in Bochim" (the ancient Greek translation has a name here). The Hebrew as it stands makes sense, so it is kept.

decisions.choice: Beth-leaphrah: "house of dust", where the people roll in the dust
decisions.reason: The name means "house of dust" or "house of the fawn", and the line plays on it: the people of Dust-town must roll in the dust, a sign of mourning (Jeremiah 6:26; Ezekiel 27:30). Its site is not known.

decisions.choice: roll yourself: the reading noted in the margin
decisions.reason: The written Hebrew text has "I have rolled myself"; the scribes noted in the margin that it is read "roll yourself", addressed to the town as a woman. The command fits the commands around it, and the margin's reading is followed.

decisions.choice: Do not let your enemies see you cry; the House of Dust; to show your sorrow (R)
decisions.reason: Readable says why there is to be no weeping in Gath, the Philistines' city (m1), gives the meaning of Beth-leaphrah so that the wordplay can be heard (m3), and says what rolling in the dust meant. These additions explain; they do not change what is said.

records.source: עִבְרִ֥י לָכֶ֛ם יוֹשֶׁ֥בֶת שָׁפִ֖יר עֶרְיָה־בֹ֑שֶׁת לֹ֤א יָֽצְאָה֙ יוֹשֶׁ֣בֶת צַֽאֲנָ֔ן מִסְפַּד֙ בֵּ֣ית הָאֵ֔צֶל יִקַּ֥ח מִכֶּ֖ם עֶמְדָּתֽוֹ׃
records.gloss: Pass on for yourselves, inhabitant of Shaphir, [in] nakedness [and] shame; not has come out [the] inhabitant of Zaanan; [the] lament of Beth-ezel will take from you its standing place.
pieces: Pass on your way, people of Shaphir, in shameful nakedness. \q The people of Zaanan have not come out. \q Beth-ezel is mourning; \q it will take its support away from you.

L.11: Pass on for yourselves, inhabitant of Shaphir, in nakedness [and] shame; \q the inhabitant of Zaanan has not come out; \q the lament of Beth-ezel— \q it will take from you its standing place.

R.11: People of Shaphir, the Lovely Town, go away into exile, naked and ashamed. \q The people of Zaanan, the Going-Out Town, do not dare to go out. \q Beth-ezel is weeping, \q and it can give you no shelter.

decisions.choice: Shaphir, Zaanan, Beth-ezel: the names play against what will happen to the towns
decisions.reason: Shaphir means "beautiful" or "pleasant", and its people will go out naked and ashamed. Zaanan sounds like the verb "come out", and its people will not come out, perhaps for fear of the enemy outside the walls. Beth-ezel may mean "house beside" or "house of nearness", and it will give no support to those who lean on it. The meaning of the names and the plays on them are not all certain.

decisions.choice: the lament of Beth-ezel will take from you its standing place: a line whose sense is not clear
alternatives: the mourning of Beth-ezel will take away its support from you
the enemy will take his stand from Beth-ezel against you
decisions.reason: The words are clear but how they fit together is not. The last word means a place to stand, and so a position or support. The line seems to say that Beth-ezel, itself in mourning, can give no help, or that the enemy will take Beth-ezel as a base. The first sense is followed here.

decisions.choice: pass on: go into exile; the towns are in the low hills near Micah's home
decisions.reason: "Pass on" means go away, probably as captives. The towns of verses 10-15 lie in the low hill country west and southwest of Jerusalem, around Micah's town of Moresheth: Gath, Lachish, Mareshah, Achzib and Adullam are known sites; Shaphir, Zaanan, Beth-ezel, Beth-leaphrah and Maroth are not. They lay on the road an army from the coast would take toward Jerusalem, as Sennacherib's army did in 701 BC.

decisions.choice: inhabitant: the people of a town, spoken of as one woman
decisions.reason: The word is a feminine singular, "she who lives in", used for the whole population of a town personified as a woman (Isaiah 12:6; Jeremiah 46:19).

decisions.choice: people of (B, R); the Lovely Town, the Going-Out Town, go away into exile, do not dare, can give you no shelter (R)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable say "people of" for "inhabitant of" (m4). Readable gives the meaning of the names so that the wordplays can be heard (m1), says what "pass on" means (m3), and gives the sense chosen for the hard last line (m2).

records.source: כִּֽי־חָ֥לָֽה לְט֖וֹב יוֹשֶׁ֣בֶת מָר֑וֹת כִּֽי־יָ֤רַד רָע֙ מֵאֵ֣ת יְהוָ֔ה לְשַׁ֖עַר יְרוּשָׁלִָֽם׃
records.gloss: For writhes for good [the] inhabitant of Maroth, for has come down calamity from Yahweh to [the] gate of Jerusalem.
pieces: The people of Maroth writhe in pain as they wait for relief, \q for disaster has come down from {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} \q to the very gate of Jerusalem.

L.12: For the inhabitant of Maroth writhes, [waiting] for good, \q for disaster has come down from {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} \q to the gate of Jerusalem.

R.12: The people of Maroth, the Bitter Town, long for something good to happen. \q But {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} has sent disaster down \q to the gates of Jerusalem.

decisions.choice: Maroth: a name meaning "bitterness", set against "good"
decisions.reason: The town's name means "bitter things". Its people hope for good, but what comes is bitter. The site is not known; it may be the Maarath of Joshua 15:59.

decisions.choice: writhes for good: waits in anguish for relief that does not come
decisions.reason: The verb usually means to writhe in pain, as a woman in labor. With "for good" it seems to mean waiting anxiously for good news or help; a related verb means to wait. Either way the people are in distress and the help they hope for is not coming.

decisions.choice: disaster has come down from the LORD: the invasion is the LORD's judgment
decisions.reason: The enemy's army is the agent; the LORD is the one who sends it, as Amos 3:6 asks: "Does disaster come to a city unless the LORD has done it?" The word "disaster" is the common word for evil, here meaning harm. The same disaster that struck Samaria reaches Jerusalem's gate (verse 9).

decisions.choice: [waiting] for good (L); as they wait for relief (B); the Bitter Town, long for something good to happen (R)
decisions.reason: The levels give the sense of the hard phrase "writhes for good" (m2). Readable gives the meaning of Maroth so that the wordplay can be heard.

records.source: רְתֹ֧ם הַמֶּרְכָּבָ֛ה לָרֶ֖כֶשׁ יוֹשֶׁ֣בֶת לָכִ֑ישׁ רֵאשִׁ֨ית חַטָּ֥את הִיא֙ לְבַת־צִיּ֔וֹן כִּי־בָ֥ךְ נִמְצְא֖וּ פִּשְׁעֵ֥י יִשְׂרָאֵֽל׃
records.gloss: Harness the chariot to the steed[s], inhabitant of Lachish; [the] beginning of sin [was] she for [the] daughter of Zion, for in you were found [the] transgressions of Israel.
pieces: Harness the horses to the chariot, people of Lachish! \q You were the beginning of sin for Daughter Zion, \q for the rebellious ways of Israel were found in you.

L.13: Harness the chariot to the steeds, inhabitant of Lachish; \q she [was] the beginning of sin for the daughter of Zion, \q for in you were found the transgressions of Israel.

R.13: People of Lachish, hitch your fastest horses to your chariots and flee! \q You were the first to lead the people of Zion into sin, \q because you copied the sins of Israel.

decisions.choice: Lachish and the steeds: a play on sound
decisions.reason: The word for steeds, fast horses for chariots, sounds like the name Lachish. Lachish was the strongest fortress city of the low hills, a city of chariots and horses. Sennacherib besieged and took it in 701 BC (2 Kings 18:14, 17), and his palace reliefs at Nineveh show the siege. The command to harness the horses is a call to flee.

decisions.choice: the beginning of sin for the daughter of Zion: Lachish led Jerusalem into Israel's sins
decisions.reason: The text does not say what Lachish's sin was. Its trust in horses and chariots may be meant, which the prophets condemn (Isaiah 31:1; Hosea 14:4; compare Deuteronomy 17:16), or a shrine where the worship of the north was copied. "The daughter of Zion" is Jerusalem and its people, spoken of as a young woman.

decisions.choice: she ... you: the line turns from speaking about Lachish to speaking to her
decisions.reason: Hebrew poetry often moves between "she" and "you" for the same person. Here Lachish is first addressed, then spoken about, then addressed again.

decisions.choice: the daughter of Zion (L); Daughter Zion (B); the people of Zion (R); transgressions (L); rebellious ways (B); sins (R); You were (B, R)
decisions.reason: The forms for the daughter of Zion and for transgression follow the wording set for the prophets. Balanced and Readable say "you" throughout, since Lachish is addressed. Readable says what harnessing the horses was for (m1).

records.source: לָכֵן֙ תִּתְּנִ֣י שִׁלּוּחִ֔ים עַ֖ל מוֹרֶ֣שֶׁת גַּ֑ת בָּתֵּ֤י אַכְזִיב֙ לְאַכְזָ֔ב לְמַלְכֵ֖י יִשְׂרָאֵֽל׃
records.gloss: Therefore you will give parting gifts to Moresheth-gath; [the] houses of Achzib [will be] a deception to [the] kings of Israel.
pieces: So you will give farewell gifts \q to Moresheth-gath. \q The houses of Achzib will prove a deception \q to the kings of Israel.

L.14: Therefore you will give parting gifts \q to Moresheth-gath; \q the houses of Achzib [will be] a deception \q to the kings of Israel.

R.14: So you must say goodbye to Moresheth-gath \q and give her parting gifts, as a father does for a daughter who marries and leaves home. \q Achzib, the Town of Lies, \q will let the kings of Israel down.

decisions.choice: parting gifts to Moresheth-gath: a farewell, with a play on the word for a bride
decisions.reason: The word for parting gifts is used of the dowry a father gave his daughter when she married and left home (1 Kings 9:16). The name Moresheth sounds like the word for "betrothed". Judah must give up Micah's home town as a father sends away his daughter: it will be lost to the enemy. "You" is a woman, Zion or Judah.

decisions.choice: Achzib ... a deception: the name sounds like the word for a stream that dries up
decisions.reason: The name Achzib sounds like a word for a deceptive brook, a stream that runs dry in summer when travelers count on it (Jeremiah 15:18). The town will fail the kings who rely on it. This Achzib is in the low hills of Judah (Joshua 15:44), not the coastal town of the same name in the north.

decisions.choice: the kings of Israel: the kings of God's people, here the kings of Judah
decisions.reason: These towns belonged to Judah, so "Israel" here is the name of the whole people of God, whose kings now reign in Jerusalem. Micah uses the name this way again (3:1, 9).

decisions.choice: say goodbye ... as a father does for a daughter who marries and leaves home; the Town of Lies; let ... down (R)
decisions.reason: Readable explains the parting gifts (m1) and gives the sense of Achzib's name (m2), since the wordplay cannot be heard otherwise.

records.source: עֹ֗ד הַיֹּרֵשׁ֙ אָ֣בִי לָ֔ךְ יוֹשֶׁ֖בֶת מָֽרֵשָׁ֑ה עַד־עֲדֻּלָּ֥םיָב֖וֹא כְּב֥וֹד יִשְׂרָאֵֽל׃
records.gloss: Again the possessor I will bring to you, inhabitant of Mareshah; to Adullam will come [the] glory of Israel.
pieces: I will once more bring a conqueror against you, \q people of Mareshah. \q The glory of Israel will come to Adullam.

L.15: I will yet bring the one who takes possession to you, \q inhabitant of Mareshah; \q the glory of Israel will come to Adullam.

R.15: People of Mareshah, whose name sounds like "conqueror", \q I will bring a conqueror against you. \q Those who are the glory of Israel will run to Adullam to hide.

decisions.choice: the one who takes possession ... Mareshah: a play on sound
decisions.reason: The word for one who takes possession, an heir or a conqueror, sounds like the name Mareshah. The town will be taken over by a new owner. "Again" may mean that, as before, an enemy will come, or simply "yet", still to come.

decisions.choice: the glory of Israel will come to Adullam: Israel's leaders will flee to hide in the caves
alternatives: Israel's God, its glory, will leave
Israel's wealth will be carried off
decisions.reason: Adullam was where David hid in a cave when he fled from Saul (1 Samuel 22:1). "The glory of Israel" most likely means its nobles and leaders, as "its glory" does in Isaiah 5:13. They will end up in hiding as David did. Some take "glory" to be Israel's God or its wealth.

decisions.choice: whose name sounds like "conqueror"; Those who are the glory of Israel will run to Adullam to hide (R)
decisions.reason: Readable lets the wordplay be heard (m1) and says what coming to Adullam means (m2).

records.source: קָרְחִ֣י וָגֹ֔זִּי עַל־בְּנֵ֖י תַּעֲנוּגָ֑יִךְ הַרְחִ֤בִי קָרְחָתֵךְ֙ כַּנֶּ֔שֶׁר כִּ֥י גָל֖וּ מִמֵּֽךְ׃ס
records.gloss: Make yourself bald and shave on account of [the] children of your delights; make wide your baldness like the eagle, for they have gone into exile from you.
pieces: Shave your head in mourning \q for the children you delight in. \q Make yourself as bald as the vulture, \q for they will be taken from you into exile.

L.16: Make yourself bald and cut off [your hair] \q for the children you delight in; \q make your baldness wide like the vulture's, \q for they have gone from you into exile.

R.16: Shave your heads to show your grief \q for the children you love. \q Make yourselves as bald as a vulture, \q because your children will be taken away as prisoners to another land.

decisions.choice: make yourself bald: shaving the head as a sign of mourning
decisions.reason: In mourning people shaved their heads or cut off their hair (Isaiah 15:2; Jeremiah 16:6; Amos 8:10), though the law forbade Israel to do it for the dead (Deuteronomy 14:1). The command is spoken to a woman, Zion or Judah as a mother, whose children are her people.

decisions.choice: the vulture: the bird usually called eagle, here the bald-headed vulture
decisions.reason: The word is the usual word for the eagle, but it also covers the great vultures. Here it is the griffon vulture, whose head and neck have only a little white down and look bald.

decisions.choice: they have gone into exile: a coming event spoken of as already done
decisions.reason: The verb is in the form for a completed action. Prophets often speak of what God has decided as if it had already happened, so certain is it. The exile is still to come.

decisions.choice: vulture (L, B, R); they have gone (L); they will be taken (B, R); Shave your heads (R)
decisions.reason: All three levels say "vulture" (m2), since an eagle is not bald. Balanced and Readable put the exile in the future (m3). Readable speaks to the people as "you" plural, since the mother addressed stands for them.
